```{r}
library(lava)
library(targeted)
```

```{r}
set.seed(4242)
sim_data <- function(n = 1000, pi = 0.5) {
  w <- rnorm(n)
  a <- rbinom(n, 1, pi)
  y <- cos(w) + w*a + a + rnorm(n)
  data.frame(y, a, w)
}
```

# Exercise 2 - One-step estimation with `targeted::cate`

## 2.1 learner R6 class: glm

Use `learner_glm` to estimate/fit a linear model to the dataset generated by
`sim_data`. The response variable is `y`, and include main effects of treatment
`a` and baseline covariate `w`, and their interactions. Inspect the estimated
model object and compare it to the object that is returned by the `glm` function
(`ref_fit` in the following). In addition, compute the in-sample mean squarred
error (MSE) between the response variable and the predictions of the estimated
learner model, i.e. the MSE of the residuals.

```{r}
d <- sim_data(n = 1e3)
ref_fit <- glm(y ~ a * w, data = d)
```

## 2.2. learner R6 class: mars

Using `learner_mars`, estimate a multivariate adaptive regression spline (MARS)
model with 5 degrees of freedom to the data. Estimate the model and compute the
MSE of the residuals. Is the MSE lower or higher than the MSE of the linear
model? Why?

Note: you don't have to specifiy interactions between `a` and `w`.

## 2.3 learner R6 class: superlearner

Using `learner_sl`, estimate a 5-fold superlearner to the data that uses the
previously defined linear and MARS model as base learners. Inspect the estimated
model and describe what you observe.

### 2.4 Estimator comparison: large sample

Estimate the ATE with the ANOVA, ANHECOVA and one-step estimator (using the
previously defined superlearner for the outcome regression model) for the
following large data sample. Compare the large sample SE and compute the
relative efficiency of the covariate adjusted estimators with respect to ANOVA
estimator.

```{r}
d_largesample <- sim_data(n = 1e5, pi = 0.5)
```

### 2.5 Estimator comparison: Monte-Carlo simulation

Compare the ANOVA, AHECOVA and one-step estimator from the previous exercise in
a Monte-Carlo simulation. Use a small sample size of `n = 200` subjects
(randomized 1:1) and perform 1e3 Monte-Carlo replications. Inspect the
simulation results and compare with the large sample estimates from the previous
exercise.

## 2.6 Binary outcome - unadjusted estimator I

Consider the following data generation process and the corresponding large
sample.

```{r}
sim_data_binary <- function(n = 300, pi = 0.5) {
  w <- rnorm(n)
  a <- rbinom(n, 1, pi)
  yb <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(1 + a + w - a * w))*1.0
  data.frame(yb, a, w)
}
d_binary <- sim_data_binary(n = 1e5)
```

The following lines implement the unadjusted estimator for the log odds ratio.

```{r}
fit_logit <- glm(yb ~ a, data = d_binary, family = binomial)
estimate(fit_logit, keep = "a")
```

Use
```{r}
lr_logit <- learner_glm(yb ~ a, family = binomial)
```

together with `cate` to implement an estimator for the log odds ratio.

## 2.7 Binary outcome - adjusted estimator

Can you directly obtain an estimate of the log odds ratio from the following
model fit?

```{r}
fit <- glm(yb ~ a + w, data = d_binary, family = binomial)
```

## 2.8 Binary outcome - adjusted estimator - one-step

Implement a one-step estimator that targets the log odds ratio and adjusts for
baseline covariate `w` (only main effect). Is the estimator more efficient than
the unadjusted estimator?

## 2.9 Binary outcome - adjusted estimator - g-computation

Can you use the logistic regression model from the previous exercise (i.e. the
`fit` object) and g-computation to estimate the log odds ratio?

Hint: `lava::expectation` can be used to implement g-computation
